voyage.name: Manly to Spit Bridge Walk
voyage.content: Along the foreshore of Sydney Harbour.

voyage.name: Bradleys Head
voyage.content: Take the ferry to Taronga Zoo wharf and then head to your right along the promontory. There's pristine bushland (almost unchanged from the time of European colonisation), quiet beaches, and knockout views across the harbour, and in the warmer months you'll spot plenty of Eastern Water Dragons, a type of large lizard. Once you reach the tip of the headland, you can either amble back to the wharf or - if you're feeling

voyage.name: Sydney Festival
voyage.content: An arts festival aiming to be international in reach, inviting acclaimed international artists to exhibit their work or perform in Sydney. A number of free outdoor events are held alongside the festival including the hugely popular Jazz in the Domain, Symphony in the Domain, and Festival First Night. Concerts held in the Domain and Hyde Park in the City Centre. The Bacardi Latin Festival in Darling Harbour is held in

voyage.name: Big Day Out
voyage.content: An Australia-wide rock/alternative music festival with a side of dance, plays to up to 60,000 Sydneysiders at a time for one or two days in late January (normally on the January 26th public holiday). Past acts have included Nirvana, the Red Hot Chili Peppers, Rage Against The Machine, Muse, the Chemical Brothers and Marilyn Manson from overseas, and Powderfinger, Regurgitator and Gerling from Australia. It normally s

voyage.name: St. Jerome's Laneway Festival
voyage.content: An alternative/indie music festival held in January/February each year (see website for upcoming dates), where bands play in laneways around the city, this festival a rather unique vibe and atmosphere. The Festival attracts both international and domestic artists, which has included such artists like Feist, Architecture in Helsinki and Born Ruffians. If you're interested in getting involved in the Sydney 'underground

voyage.name: Chinese New Year
voyage.content: Widely celebrated by Sydney's Chinese community, with the centre of festivities being at Chinatown. Look out for Lion dancing, Dragonboat races at Darling Harbour, and of course plenty of good food.

voyage.name: Sydney Gay and Lesbian Mardi Gras
voyage.content: A festival organised by and for the gay community. It includes sports, cultural and arts events that run throughout February, culminating in the Mardi Gras parade in Darlinghurst on the first Saturday of March each year. The festival began in 1978 as a street protest when homosexuality was illegal, and participants were violently arrested and shamed. Since then, it has grown into a huge celebration with large crowds,

voyage.name: Sydney French Film Festival
voyage.alt: The Alliance Francaise French Film Festival
voyage.content: Offers an impressive and ambitious panoramic view of contemporary French cinema, screening the films at Palace Academy Twin in Oxford St, Darlinghurst, Verona in Paddington & Norton Street in Leichhardt.

voyage.name: Cockatoo Island Festival
voyage.content: Where lots of friendly people enjoy a fabulous mixture of music and culture while discovering one of Sydney's best kept secrets.

voyage.name: Royal Easter Show
voyage.content: Is the major agricultural show in New South Wales, and is held around Easter each year at Sydney Olympic Park. Farmers from all over the state come to show their prize produce. But it isn't just an agricultural show: a huge number of amusement ride operators set up for the show as well, together with vendors of the worst kind of child baiting junk food: fairy floss and deep fried hot dogs (known as "dagwood dogs" or

voyage.name: Sydney German Film Festival
voyage.alt: Audi Festival of German Films in Australia
voyage.content: Shows contemporary German films.

voyage.name: Vivid Sydney
voyage.content: Sydney's historic and landmark building illuminated. The best sights are around Circular Quay with the Opera House making an especially fantastic canvas. Martin Place is full of light shows and food stalls. And Barrangaroo laneways are decorated also. Some suburbs also have smaller light shows, including the centres of Chatswood and Parramatta. Expect large crowds and make sure to do some preparation – lots of road c

voyage.name: Biennale of Sydney
voyage.content: A contemporary arts and multimedia festival held in winter in even numbered years.

voyage.name: Sydney Film Festival
voyage.content: Shows over 200 movies in 16 days, including an enormous number of Australian and international movies, most of which will premiere at the festival.

voyage.name: Arabic Film Festival
voyage.content: Shows dozens of movies over a week at Parramatta.

voyage.name: The Rocks Aroma Festival
voyage.content: A homage to Sydney's love affair with coffee during a cold winter's day. Lots of artisan coffee stalls throughout the Rocks area.

voyage.name: Sydney Fringe Festival
voyage.content: Features fringe art in the form of film, TV, performance and sport.

voyage.name: Lavazza Italian Film Festival
voyage.content: Showcases the finest that Italian cinema has to offer, picking contemporary films from the vibrant Rome International Film Festival to the more established events such as the prestigious Berlinale and the world-famous Cannes Film Festival; and a selection of Italian Classics from the archives of the Cinecittà Studios in Rome.

voyage.name: Sydney Underground Film Festival
voyage.content: The festival programs unique, quality independent films that transgress the status quo and challenge the conservative conventions of film making. The festival is devoted to renewing local interest in independent and experimental film as part of an international underground film culture and aims to change an ingrained culture of cinematic complacency and revitalise an enthusiasm for cinema.

voyage.name: Crave Sydney
voyage.content: Showcases the city's best restaurants, established and up-and-coming young chefs, food and wine culture. "Hats off dinners", the night noodle markets at Hyde Park, and hands-on cooking classes. Food festivals and markets all around Sydney

voyage.name: Musica Viva Festival
voyage.content: Sydney's premier chamber music festival. The festival presents a rich feast of masterworks and musical treasures played by some of the world's finest practitioners, interspersed with music of different cultures.

voyage.name: Sculpture by the Sea
voyage.content: Join tens of thousands of Sydneysiders as they take a leisurely walk between Bondi Beach and Tamarama Beach to admire the numerous larger than life sculptures set up at both beaches and along the walk. Bring a camera to take snaps of the weird and wonderful exhibits.

voyage.name: Carols in the Domain
voyage.content: Held annually in the Domain in the city centre on the last Saturday before Christmas. Attracts around 100,000 people (so plan to get in there early for a good spot) with candles sing along as night falls.

voyage.name: New Year's Eve
voyage.content: Features massive displays of pyrotechnics around Sydney Harbour and the Harbour Bridge (including fireworks shot from the bridge itself). There are two shows, a "family show" at 9PM, and the major fireworks display at midnight. Immediately following the 9PM Family Fireworks, the spectacular Harbour of Light Parade begins. Over 50 vessels make a majestic passage on a 15km circuit around the Harbour, featuring illumina

voyage.name: KVB Kunlun
voyage.content: This large trading company mainly deals with businesses and big amounts but they also exchange money for individuals with smaller amounts. They charge you $10 if you exchange under $2,000 but their rate is so competitive that it's still worth going there for changing a few hundreds. They have by far the best rate in Sydney. Be prepared to wait as some travellers have been reporting to be there for over an hour.

voyage.name: Spinway
voyage.price: $11 an hour, $22 for a half day (4 hour rental) or $33 for a full day (24 hour rental)
voyage.content: bicycle rental stations in the Hilton Hotel and the Intercontinental Hotel available to guests and the public

voyage.name: Sydney Opera House
voyage.content: This world heritage listed icon on the harbour is one of Sydney's most beautiful and unusual buildings; its sail-shaped structure, designed by Jørn Utzon, is world famous, and it is the only structure in the world to have been designated a UNESCO World Heritage Site during the lifetime of its architect. The Opera House hosts most of Sydney's major classical music and opera events. You can walk all around the building

voyage.name: Circular Quay
voyage.content: The hub of the Sydney Harbour between the bridge and Opera House and is a vibrant, bustling place home to many buskers, the ferry terminal, overseas passenger terminal, as well as the Museum of Contemporary Art. It is one of the main areas of the annual Vivid festival.

voyage.name: Sydney Tower
voyage.content: Towering above the city of Sydney since 1981, when it became the tallest structure in the city, the Sydney Tower reaches a total height of 305 m — great views are available from the 250-m-high viewing level. The tower is Australia's tallest free-standing structure and the second highest observation tower in the Southern Hemisphere after the Sky Tower in Auckland). The trip up to the observation deck includes a short

voyage.name: St. Mary's Cathedral
voyage.content: The Catholic Sydney diocese's cathedral, built in 1868.

voyage.name: Queen Victoria Building
voyage.content: The site of a market place since 1810, its current Romanesque facade was completed in 1896 and was extensively restored in the late 1980s as a prestigious shopping centre. The Christmas tree around Christmas time reaches through all the floors to the full height of the building. It contains a variety of small shops selling luxury fashion and cafes. On the top floor is a large albeit very cramped model and toy shop. T

voyage.name: The Strand Arcade
voyage.content: A fine example of Victorian Architecture, established 1891, and is one of the few remaining Victorian shopping arcades in the world. For the past 20 years or so, it has been a major shopping destination, well known for the large number of Australian designers it showcases. Many well recognized Australian labels in fashion and jewellery are based here, such as Alannah Hill, Zimmerman, and Victoria Buckley Jewellery.

voyage.name: Powerhouse Museum (Temporarily closed)
voyage.content: The Powerhouse Museum is closed (as of February 2024) for refurbishment and does not have an estimated reopening date. Usually, it has a variety of permanent and temporary exhibitions including the King's Cinema, an intact art deco cinema, Locomotive No 1, Experimentations, Ecologic, the Strasbourg Clock, the Steam Revolution and Interface. There is a cafe and museum shop.

voyage.name: Trim the Cat
voyage.content: A bronze statue of Trim, the cat who accompanied Matthew Flinders on his voyages to circumnavigate and map the coastline of Australia from 1801 to 1803.

voyage.name: The Art Gallery of New South Wales
voyage.price: Free admission with charges to some 'feature' exhibitions
voyage.content: the leading museum of art in New South Wales and Sydney, and one of Australia's foremost cultural institutions. It holds significant collections of Australian art, and presents nearly forty exhibitions annually. British Victorian art, along with smaller holdings of Dutch, French and Italian painters of the 16th, 17th and 18th centuries, and a collection of modern British masters, European modernists and European clas

voyage.name: Museum of Sydney
voyage.price: Admission adult , child / concessions , family , members free (run by the Historic Houses Trust)
voyage.hours: Daily (closed Christmas Day and Good Fri)
voyage.content: Built on the site of the first Government House, erected in 1788 by Governor Arthur Phillip and demolished in 1846. The remains of the building were excavated after rediscovery in 1983 and the original foundations can now be viewed through glass floor panels in the museum. Fascinating changing exhibitions of art and photography, films and state-of-the-art technology spin stories of colonial life, Aboriginal culture,

voyage.name: Hyde Park Barracks
voyage.hours: Daily , closed Good Fri and Christmas Day
voyage.content: Built in 1818-1819. Constructed by convicts and housed by them, the Hyde Park Barracks provided housing for convicts working in government employment around Sydney from 1819 until its closure in 1848. Interior is restored with exhibits depicting the furnishings and life of the time. Inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List.

voyage.name: State Library of New South Wales
voyage.content: Includes a large exhibition space with changing artistic, historical and cultural exhibits. The Mitchell Reading Room is a historical large open book-lined room, and worth a look inside. The reference library is a modern addition, and really only of interest for research. The library collection includes a copy of every volume published in New South Wales, and many rare texts. There is a cafe on the ground floor near

voyage.name: Government House
voyage.content: A stately home in the Botanic Gardens. The official residence of the Governor of New South Wales (the state's representative for the British Monarch). Open to the public Fridays & weekends.

voyage.name: Reserve Bank of Australia Museum
voyage.hours: Temporarily closed as of June 2025; otherwise open Mon-Fri 10AM-5PM, except bank holidays
voyage.content: Hosted by the Reserve Bank of Australia in its city headquarters, this museum displays Australian bank notes and currency from the earliest issues to the present day. Interesting but basic. Drop in for 15 min or so if you are passing by Martin Place.

voyage.name: Justice and Police Museum
voyage.content: Built as a police station to Court in 1856, and closed in 1886, the museum has now been restored to its 1890s facade displaying its theme of crime and punishment.

voyage.name: ANZAC Memorial
voyage.content: A large war memorial in the middle of the city, built after World War I. It is a focus of military memorial events in New South Wales and includes a museum which covers the experiences of NSW citizens who have served in the Australian military.

voyage.name: Customs House
voyage.content: A historic building, and imposing building. You can imagine it looking out over the port of Sydney (if you can equally imagine the absence of the Cahill Expressway). A large diorama of the Sydney area which you can walk over is on display in the foyer. The Sydney City Library occupies the building, and sometimes has exhibitions. Free.

voyage.name: Royal Botanic Gardens
voyage.price: There are no access charges to enter the Botanic Gardens (except for the tropical pyramid)
voyage.hours: The gardens are open from sunrise to sunset. It is fully fenced, so take care not to get locked in at closing time
voyage.content: One of Sydney's greatest assets, from in front of the State Art Gallery, out to Mrs Macquaries chair, across to Farm Cove and onto the Sydney Opera House. The Gardens back onto the historic Sydney Hospital and Parliament House. This is the oldest scientific institution in the country and home to an outstanding collection of plants from Australia and overseas. The Domain surrounds the Royal Botanic Gardens. The walk a

voyage.name: Palm Grove Centre
voyage.content: Visitors centre, a restaurant, a cafe and a souvenir shop.

voyage.name: Mrs Macquarie's Chair
voyage.content: This park area has magnificent views of the harbour.

voyage.name: The Domain
voyage.price: There are no entrance fees to the Domain, however at times the Domain is used for events and the event organisers may charge admission fees or impose other access controls to the specific areas annexed for those events
voyage.content: In colonial times this land was the Governor’s buffer of privacy between his residence and the penal colony. Roads and paths were constructed through the Domain by 1831 to allow public access. Since that time it has remained a place for the people to breath and relax. The Domain surrounds the Royal Botanic Gardens. In times past has been a site of often quite colourful public oratory and site of public rallies and de

voyage.name: Hyde Park
voyage.content: An extensive city centre park of a formal design tradition dissected by Park St, elongated in layout and containing a large fountain (Archibald Fountain) towards the northern end and the Anzac War Memorial at the south - a favourite with city workers at lunchtime, joggers and sunbakers. The park occasionally hosts public and private events and functions.

voyage.name: Captain Cook Cruises
voyage.content: have regular cruises from Wharf 1 at the Quay.

voyage.name: Sydney Ferries Cruises
voyage.content: Sydney Ferries run regular cruises. Just look on the main timetable boards at the Quay, and buy your tickets from any Sydney Ferries ticket office.

voyage.name: Sydney Opera House
voyage.content: The Sydney Opera House is one of the most iconic 20th-century buildings in the world. Inaugurated in 1973, the Sydney Opera House also has dedicated theatres for drama including the Drama Theatre, the Playhouse, and The Studio. Student rush tickets are often available for the current day's performances, only at the box office at the Opera House (usually these are single tickets, spread around the theatre).

voyage.name: Theatre Royal
voyage.content: Home to many international productions during their stay in Australia.

voyage.name: State Theatre
voyage.content: Hosts a range of events and performances, particularly international comedy acts and musicians. The building itself is heritage-listed, and has a lavish interior dating back to 1929.

voyage.name: The Basement
voyage.content: Famous place for small gigs in Sydney. Attracts some leading acts.

voyage.name: Event Cinemas
voyage.content: Large cinema complex with a variety of different screens, including 4D and VMAX. This is the only multiplex in the city of Sydney itself, although some of the latest films can also be found at the nearby IMAX on Darling Harbour.

voyage.name: The Art Gallery of New South Wales
voyage.content: Free cinema on Wednesdays & Sundays, but usually old films.

voyage.name: Aboriginal Bush Tucker Tour
voyage.price: $30 for adults, $20 for children 7 and older, free for children under 7
voyage.content: A walk around the Royal Botanic Garden with an Aboriginal guide who will tell you about native plants that have been used by Aboriginal Australians for generations, as food, medicine, and tools. You can sample a few on the way, including fruits and herbs. Book in advance.

voyage.name: Queen Victoria Building
voyage.content: The building is an attraction in itself. The site of a market place since 1810, its current Romanesque facade was completed in 1896 and was extensively restored in the late 1980s as a prestigious shopping centre. 5 Floors of shopping. Don't miss the Christmas tree to Christmas, going through all the levels. Fashion, books, cafes, and a range of specialty and gift shops.

voyage.name: Galleries Victoria
voyage.content: The modern answer to the historic QVB opposite. Some fashion and food, but also electronics, computer games, and gifts.

voyage.name: Strand Arcade
voyage.content: The last of the Victorian arcades to be completed (1891) in Sydney, home to a number of shopping levels featuring design, fashion, antiques and jewellery (the arcade links George Street with the Pitt Street Mall).

voyage.name: Westfield Sydney
voyage.content: 7 levels of Myer department store and a food court (level 1) on west side; hundreds of specialty and fashion stores plus an upscale food court (level 5) on east side. Entry to Sydney Tower at level 5 east side. Connects underground to the Queen Victoria Building from level 1 west side.

voyage.name: David Jones
voyage.content: The city stores of this illustrious department store are on Elizabeth Street (main store, women's fashion) and Market Street (men's fashion, homewares, food store). In operation since 1838, David Jones is not only Australia's oldest department store, but also the oldest department store anywhere in the world still trading under its original name.

voyage.name: MLC Centre
voyage.content: A shopping arcade, primarily focused on luxury clothes and accessories, and a food court downstairs. Belinda in the MLC Centre stocks European designers that don't have standalone stores in Australia. Has some reasonable cafes in the courtyard facing Martin Place.

voyage.name: Mecca Coffee
voyage.content: Very good tasting coffee with a massive queue of office workers in the morning. Additionally, they sell specialty coffee blends online.

voyage.name: Fix St James
voyage.content: A restaurant/wine bar open for breakfast, lunch and dinner. The food is Italian-influenced but definitely 'Modern Australian'. Has a very interesting wine list with many available by the glass.

voyage.name: Sydney Madang
voyage.content: Tasty and inexpensive Korean barbecue and other dishes. Open until early in the morning.

voyage.name: BBQ City
voyage.content: If you can't find Madang, and you're in the mood for Korean, there's always the Sydney institution, BBQ city, a big brightly-lit upstairs restaurant, with Korean pop stars dancing incessantly on TV screens around the room. It's quick, cheap, delicious, and open late.

voyage.name: Ash St Cellar
voyage.content: Ash St Cellar is a Melbourne-style laneway bar just behind the Ivy complex. The food is (Sydney style) tapas influenced share plates, the wine and beer list is good and the atmosphere is great. No bookings and not open on weekends.

voyage.name: Young Alfred
voyage.address: Customs House, Ground Floor, 31 Alfred St
voyage.content: Famous Sydney pizza and pasta joint very conveniently located just next to Circular Quay. The owners used to own a very famous pizza restaurant on Oxford St in Paddington but have relocated here. Pizzas are not traditional Italian but very good nonetheless. Main courses $20-32, pizzas $24-32.

voyage.name: Nazimi
voyage.content: Authentic Japanese food, with different options on the menu to a lot of places. Customers are packed in, but the service is very friendly.

voyage.name: Makoto Sushi Bar
voyage.content: Decent sushi bar, higher quality than your standard sushi train. Makoto offers sushi, sashimi, along with a range of small cooked dishes. Open 7 days, with dinner starting from 6PM.

voyage.name: Ichi Ban Boshi
voyage.content: Fantastic ramen soup. The Tantanamen (Spicy sesame base pork ramen) is a very large and delicious soup. Restaurant gets very busy at any time past 11:30AM till around 2PM. Expect to wait 10-20 minutes for a table in the peak times.

voyage.name: Munich Brauhaus
voyage.content: Large German restaurant that is part of a chain with authentic Bavarian beer and somewhat authentic German food.

voyage.name: Cafe Sydney
voyage.content: Tucked away atop the Customs House right next to Circular Quay, Cafe Sydney sneaks under the radar of most casual visitors, but the outdoor seating here has some of the best Sydney Harbour views around and draws plenty of locals as well. The pricy but well-crafted food is Mod Oz, try the Bay Bug salad or the tarragon gnocchi and expect to pay around $100/head for a full meal. There's also a bar area with complicated

voyage.name: Est
voyage.hours: Mon-Fri lunch and dinner, Sat dinner only
voyage.content: The chef at Est, Peter Doyle, has had a 30-year stint as one of the top chefs in Australia. French-influenced modern Australian cuisine with an emphasis on using the best seasonal produce.

voyage.name: Rockpool Bar and Grill
voyage.content: Part of the Neil Perry empire (which also includes Rockpool at the Rocks, Spice Temple underneath the Bar and Grill and a bar and grill in Melbourne), this restaurant serves superb modern Australian cuisine in a spectacular art deco setting (that reputedly cost $30 million+ to fit out). As you might expect, the steaks are the highlight but the wine list is also one of the best in Australia. For a more budget option,

voyage.name: O Bar
voyage.content: Spectacular views over Sydney from this revolving bar at the top of the 1970s iconic Australia Square office tower, a stylish makeover of the old Summit Restaurant. Designer cocktails while the entire level revolves slowly over 90 minutes. Floor to ceiling windows means that you can gaze from your Kubrick-2001-inspired seating and decor to the city below. Consistently highly reviewed. Cocktails average $20 a glass.

voyage.name: Gilt Lounge Bar
voyage.content: In QT Sydney Hotel, opened 2013. Extensive wine and cocktail list in modern eames-style setting.

voyage.name: Cantina OK
voyage.content: Small bar specialising in mezcal and cocktails, which has appeared twice on The World’s 50 Best Bars list.

voyage.name: 3 Wise Monkeys Pub
voyage.content: The 3 Wise Monkeys is a very popular pub with a younger crowd, only a block south of Town Hall station in the cinema district. It has live music seven nights a week.

voyage.name: Metro Theatre
voyage.content: The metro, in the cinema district near Town Hall, is a live music venue for Australian and overseas acts. Usually standing room only, and active mosh pit at the front, with an active vibe.

voyage.name: The Music
voyage.content: A free, weekly music publication. You can find a copy at most music stores around the city and the inner suburbs.

voyage.name: Park Regis City Centre
voyage.content: The hotel is surrounded by Sydney’s best shopping, entertainment and sightseeing. Views from the 45th floor rooftop pool and observation deck are guaranteed to leave a lasting impression.

voyage.name: Rendezvous Studio Hotel Sydney Central
voyage.content: A vibrant hotel and accommodation solution, combines clean lines, contemporary style and a personal feel.

voyage.name: QT Sydney
voyage.content: Opened in October 2012. Luxury designer hotel. Emphasis on art and fashion. Located on Market Street in the CBD. Across from Pitt Street Shopping Mall.

voyage.name: Four Seasons Sydney
voyage.price: From $300, keep an eye out for promotional package deals
voyage.content: An older but immaculately maintained five-star hotel with superlative service. Regular rooms are small, but have direct views of the Opera House, and it doesn't get much better than this locationwise.

voyage.name: Intercontinental Sydney
voyage.content: Close to Circular Quay and the Royal Botanic Gardens.

voyage.name: Jamison Sydney
voyage.content: Jamison Sydney is in the north of the CBD, close to The Rocks, Circular Quay, the Opera House and the Sydney Harbour Bridge.

voyage.name: Sydney Harbour Marriott
voyage.content: The hotel offers Opera House and Harbour Bridge view rooms along with a gym, day spa, restaurant, outdoor bar and coffee/cocktail lounge. The hotel also enjoys one of the best locations in Sydney.

voyage.name: Radisson Blu Plaza Hotel Sydney
voyage.content: A very Scandinavian-style refurbishment of an historic stone faced building. Good sized rooms, powerful showers and wide range of amenities. Concierges helpful. Breakfast OK but not sparkling. Hallways have stuffy air.

voyage.name: Sheraton on the Park
voyage.price: Rooms with one king sized bed: $260-300 per night
voyage.content: One of the nicest 5-star hotels in Sydney. It is opposite the Hyde Park (ask for a Park view room to take full advantage of the location, but note these are usually more expensive than the City view rooms) and the staff are really friendly.

voyage.name: The Westin
voyage.content: Superb rooms, particularly the Heritage rooms.

voyage.name: West Hotel Sydney, Curio Collection by Hilton
voyage.content: The hotel is equipped with 182 designer rooms, botanically inspired restaurant and bar, and a wedding venue.

voyage.name: RAN Heritage Centre
voyage.content: Museum dedicated to the Royal Australian Navy.

voyage.name: Southeast Bridge Pylon
voyage.price: Admission is $13 adults, $6.50 children under 13, and free for children under 7
voyage.hours: The pylon is open 10AM-5PM every day except Christmas Day
voyage.content: Climb up to the Pylon Lookout. Entrance is from the pedestrian walkway on Bradfield Highway approach to the bridge. (There is no entrance at the base of the Pylon in Dawes Point.) As you climb the 200 steps within the pylon, you pass 3 levels of exhibits describing pictorially the history of the bridge. The view at the Pylon Lookout is as good as from the Sydney tower, maybe better, as you are out in the open air and

voyage.name: Bridge Climb
voyage.price: Standard rates are around $360 adults and $160 children, with extra cost for special times
voyage.content: You can climb to the top of the arch of the bridge. For those who are good with heights and enjoy a spectacular view of the harbour, there are organised climbs to the top of the bridge. This climb is more demanding than climbing a set of stairs, although it is not so demanding as the name implies. You will be fitted with special climbing suits and secured by safety tethers, you must be 10 years old or over to take th

voyage.name: Natural Wanders
voyage.price: $150 for one person or $120/person if two or more
voyage.content: The Bridge Paddle tour takes you kayak paddling under the bridge on a tour exploring the northern shore. They do this as a private tour - just you and the guide.

voyage.name: Cadman's Cottage
voyage.hours: Mon-Fri 9:30AM-4:30PM, Sat Sun 10AM-4:30PM, closed Christmas and Good Fri
voyage.content: The last relic of the small, relatively plain buildings that once ringed Sydney Cove in the early colonial period, this small sandstone cottage was built in 1815-1816. The building has survived largely because of constant government or institutional ownership. Restoration began in 1972 and the building is now used as an information centre by the National Parks and Wildlife Service. The Cottage was built by the water

voyage.name: Argyle Cut
voyage.content: Follow Argyle St through this historic sandstone road cutting made between 1843 and 1867, made with the effort of both convict and paid labour. The sights and sounds of the convict labour, still bound in chains and working only with crude tools, horrified the locals and the cutting was abandoned after just three years. A long interlude lasted before the city council eventually linked Millers Point and The Rocks toget

voyage.name: Garrison Church
voyage.content: The colony's first military church, it is still an active Anglican church.

voyage.name: Museum of Contemporary Art Australia
voyage.content: Art museum focusing on work by contemporary Australian artists. Housed in a fabulous 1930s art deco building, former location of the Maritime Services Board and facing onto the western side of Circular Quay and Sydney Cove, the MCA has been dedicated since its opening in 1991 to showcasing great works of modern and contemporary art in all media. One wing is newer, contemporary architecture; the other is a historic bu

voyage.name: Sydney Observatory
voyage.price: Daytime admission is free. For night tours adults $20-22 and children $14-15
voyage.hours: Daily 10AM–5PM. Closed Good Fri, Christmas Day and Boxing Day.
voyage.content: Australia's oldest observatory. It has a variety of exhibitions, a “beanbag planetarium” and of course, telescopes. The parks and views of the harbour from the Observatory Hill are exceptional. It's worth a visit even if you have no interest in astronomy and are not even going into the building. You can book a night tour guided by an astronomer, where you're allowed to use the telescope and see what is visible during

voyage.name: Susannah Place
voyage.hours: Daily 2-5PM (closed Christmas Day and Good Fri) - guided tours only
voyage.content: Owned by Sydney Living Museums. Built in 1844, Susannah Place Museum preserves a row of four terrace houses that incorporate a re-created 1915 corner store, providing a rare opportunity to construct patterns of domestic working class life from the mid 1840s to the late 20th century. It is evidence of the rich community that once existed in The Rocks. The modest interiors and rear yards illustrate the restrictions of

voyage.name: National Trust Centre
voyage.price: Free entry, prices apply for special exhibitions
voyage.address: Observatory Hill, Upper Fort Street, Millers Point
voyage.content: The headquarters of National Trust NSW, it was once a military hospital and state school. The SH Erwin Gallery is located within and hosts exhibitions every now and then.

voyage.name: Marrinawi Cove
voyage.content: Free swimming spot in the harbour! Shark netting installed. Free showers as well, but no other facilities. Cafes are close by, however.

voyage.name: The Wharf Theatre
voyage.content: Pier Walsh Bay, on an old, renovated finger wharf. There is a bar and restaurant open during the show and at intermission. Booking for the restaurant is a good idea.

voyage.name: Sydney Theatre
voyage.content: A larger, more modern theatre across the road from the water, and around 300 m further up Hickson Road. It has a bar open before shows and at intermission. It is a larger theatre than the wharf theatres, seating nearly 1000.

voyage.name: Bonza Bike Tours
voyage.content: Offers a range of guided bicycle tours that start in The Rocks and take in various precincts throughout Sydney. Bicycle hire and bike rentals are also available.

voyage.name: Sydney Bike Tours
voyage.content: Hire a bike and explore one of three self-guided bicycle tours. Bike the Sydney Harbour Bridge, explore the city's parklands, and ride to the Sydney Fish Markets for lunch.

voyage.name: The Rocks Ghost Tours
voyage.price: Between $39 and $55 per person for standard nightly tours. Private group tours cost more
voyage.content: Tours depart daily 7:45PM. It is wise to book ahead.

voyage.name: Rocks Market
voyage.content: The far northern end of George Street, open every weekend, Sa Su 10AM-5PM, managed by the Sydney Harbour Foreshore Authority, info. With over 150 stalls under colourful canopies, pick and choose from art and crafts, jewellery, photography, indigenous artwares and tasty food stalls.

voyage.name: Pancakes on the Rocks
voyage.content: A Rocks institution since 1975, serving mouth-watering pancakes stacked high. This restaurant can still draw queues that go right along the stairs, and have waiters that hand out menus to the people in the queue. The popularity likely as much due to the scene, as to the food, and certainly popular with the teenage crowd.

voyage.name: La Renaissance Patisserie Francaise
voyage.content: A sweet little cake shop serving the finest handmade cakes, pastries, savouries and chocolates in The Rocks. Also does Teas and Coffees.

voyage.name: Fortune of War
voyage.content: Makes a claim to be Sydney's oldest pub and continuously licensed since 1830. A wide range of beers on tap, including Guinness and a variety of Australian brews. Very popular amongst office workers and can get cosy in the evenings and at weekends, not helped by its small size.

voyage.name: The Orient
voyage.content: Housed in an historic building of the 1850s. Multiple floors, dance floor.

voyage.name: The Mercantile Hotel
voyage.content: Irish pubs, Guinness on tap.

voyage.name: Hero of Waterloo
voyage.content: Built in 1843, this sandstone and timber pub has a great colonial ambiance

voyage.name: Lord Nelson Brewery Hotel
voyage.content: Established in 1842 in this very sandstone building on the corner of Kent Street and Argyle Street, just far enough away from the Rocks to avoid the worst of the tourist crush, the Lord Nelson is Sydney's oldest pub that has been continually operating in the same premises. They're particularly well known for their microbrews including their flagship Three Sheets pale ale and Nelson's Blood porter. The downstairs pub

voyage.name: Blu Bar on 36
voyage.content: Amazing views of Sydney Harbour.

voyage.name: The Bar
voyage.content: Cosy, comfortable hotel bar with a quieter ambience and views. Pricey.

voyage.name: The Australian
voyage.content: The Australian boasts a prodigious range of Australian beers, and very good gourmet pizzas (ranging from vegetarian to crocodile). As the Australian coat of arms features a kangaroo and an emu, you shouldn't be surprised that the "Coat of Arms" pizza contains meat from these animals. Can be hard to get a table between around 6PM and around 9PM. Usually attracts a more mature and quiet crowd than the pubs closer to Ge

voyage.name: The Russell Hotel
voyage.price: Rooms from $250 per night twin share
voyage.content: Boutique Bed and Breakfast in the heart of the Rocks.

voyage.name: Harbour Rocks Hotel
voyage.content: 4-star, boutique hotel housed in a 150-year-old heritage listed building which is on the site of Sydney's first hospital.

voyage.name: The Australian Heritage Hotel
voyage.content: Pub-style accommodation.

voyage.name: The Langham
voyage.content: The Langham in Sydney has a European feel to it. Located on a quiet part of Kent St, a couple of min to walk to the Rocks, across from the Observatory park.

voyage.name: Park Hyatt Sydney
voyage.content: Quite possibly Sydney's best hotel, the Park Hyatt has a superb setting, positioned on the harbour shore at Dawes Point next to the Harbour Bridge and directly opposite the Opera House situated across Sydney Cove. If you get a harbour view room, the view probably doesn't get any better. Rooms start from about $800/night and are rarely if ever discounted.

voyage.name: Sebel Pier One Sydney Hotel
voyage.content: Low rise, absolute waterfront hotel, just to the west of the Harbour Bridge. Has panoramic Sydney Harbour views a contemporary chic hotel based on a heritage wharf. Rooms cost $300-400 a night.

voyage.name: Shangri-La Hotel
voyage.content: A high-rise, modern hotel if you want to splash out. Beautiful views over the harbour, fantastic service, located at the Quay.The corner suites are spectacular, ideal for honeymoon accommodation.

voyage.name: Quay Grand Suites Sydney
voyage.content: Luxury accommodation with harbour view rooms and spa baths.

voyage.name: Quay West Suites Sydney
voyage.content: Views of Sydney Harbour Bridge and Sydney Opera House.

voyage.name: SEA LIFE Sydney Aquarium
voyage.price: Adults $44, child $25, various concessions and family tickets available. Save 15-20% online
voyage.content: A massive aquarium. In addition to various display tanks (penguins, platypus, various fish species), it has three underwater walks where visitors walk in glass corridors underneath and between the dugongs, sharks, rays and tropical fish. There is a 2-minute "penguin ride" in a small boat, heavily advertised but underwhelming. Consider going on a weekday evening, to avoid some of the crowds.

voyage.name: Sonic X & Littlest Pet Shop 2012
voyage.content: If you don't have time to get out to Taronga Zoo, then this offers the chance to see Australian wildlife close to the city.

voyage.name: Pyrmont Bridge
voyage.hours: Opens Sat Sun and public holidays at 10:30AM, noon, 1PM, 2PM and 3PM (weather permitting)
voyage.content: The Pyrmont Bridge is an old swing bridge, that used to be a main thouroughfare into Sydney. Now it only carries pedestrians across the harbour. See the centre span swing and a tall ship leave the bay. Tours of the control cab by appointment.

voyage.name: Chinese Garden of Friendship
voyage.content: Modelled on the typical private gardens of the Ming Dynasty, the garden offers an insight into Chinese heritage and culture. A centrepiece of the gardens is the Dragon Wall, guarded by two imperial dragons, with the brown dragon representing Guangdong and the blue dragon New South Wales, playing with the pearl of friendship.

voyage.name: Darling Harbour (Harbourside) Fireworks
voyage.content: Harbourside Fireworks are on from 8:30PM every Saturday on Cockle Bay Harbour. They last for only 15 minutes but are fun to watch especially if you have kids. A good trick is to get a balcony seat around some of the restaurants and you can see the fireworks whilst having dinner or drinks.

voyage.name: Crown Sydney Sky Deck
voyage.content: Sydney's tallest building, the Crown Casino, offers free guided tours of its 83rd-floor observation deck perched 250 meters above the harbour, with great views towards the Opera House. The catch is that there's exactly one tour at 8 AM on weekdays only, with capacity for just 10 people. Tickets for the following week are released every Monday and are usually snapped up in minutes.

voyage.name: Madame Tussaud's
voyage.content: It features a variety of personalities, mostly Australians such as Hugh Jackman.

voyage.name: Australian National Maritime Museum
voyage.price: Galleries & exhibitions: $7 adult, $3.50 child & concession, $17 family / free entry to permanent galleries on first Thursday of the month. Additional charges for vessels
voyage.content: Two floors of internal exhibits, outlining the maritime role in Australia's history. Houses significant full scale exhibits. Outside there are ships and submarines to explore.

voyage.name: Sydney Heritage Fleet
voyage.content: The Fleet restores and operates a number of historic vessels including the barque James Craig. In 2003 the International Congress of Maritime Museums gave the James Craig the Maritime Heritage Award. The offices, model workshop, some displayed boats, and the library are on Wharf 7 located in Darling Harbour. The James Craig is alongside the wharf.

voyage.name: Tumbalong Park
voyage.content: At first look, appears a bit like an oval, but is actually a large open space with a stage for outdoor performances. Something going on here most weekends, and a good place to lay out a picnic blanket

voyage.name: International Convention Centre Sydney
voyage.content: Sydney's main exhibition and convention centre. This new convention centre was built to replace the old convention centre and the Sydney Entertainment Centre to the tune of $1.5 billion. The centre is used for exhibitions across the year, as well as for music acts, talks and concerts in the two large theaters on either side of Exhibition centre.

voyage.name: Strike Bowling Bar
voyage.content: Bowling, Karaoke, music, drinks

voyage.name: IMAX
voyage.content: In Darling Harbour, the Sydney IMAX was completely rebuilt and reopened in 2024.

voyage.name: Magistic Cruises
voyage.content: Magistic Cruises has Sydney Harbour dinner cruise, wine cruises, lunch cruise and sightseeing cruises.

voyage.name: Sydney Show Boats
voyage.content: Showboat Cruise has a 3-course dinner cruise on Sydney Harbour, where an Australian cast performs a Live Cabaret show between each course.

voyage.name: Captain Cook Cruises
voyage.content: The Sydney Harbour Explorer Cruise allows hopping on and off at a number of attractions, or a 1½-hour cruise of the harbour. Coffee cruise departs at 10AM and 3PM.

voyage.name: Matilda Cruises
voyage.content: Seafood lunch cruise.

voyage.name: Sydney Fish Market
voyage.content: The largest seafood market in the Southern Hemisphere, which moved to shiny, modern digs in early 2026. The restaurants here are by and large tourist traps, but the fresh fish is excellent: grab a selection of sashimi or some of the precooked treats (prawns, crab, lobster) and a bottle of vino, then head across the road to Wentworth Park for a picnic. They also run a well-regarded cooking school. Sydneysiders stock u

voyage.name: Muum Maam
voyage.content: Inventive, upmarket Thai street food with dishes like Moreton Bay bugs betel leaf wraps and tom yum martinis.

voyage.name: Blackbird Cafe
voyage.content: Moderately priced and popular cafe one level up at Cockle Bay Wharf.

voyage.name: Chinta Ria
voyage.content: Indian influence. Great food and value for the location. Casual atmosphere, with kitch chairs, incense, and a large Buddha at the entrance.

voyage.name: Nick's Seafood Restaurant
voyage.content: Seafood focus, as the name suggests.

voyage.name: Sydney Fish Markets
voyage.price: $23-40 for a decent feed with a drink
voyage.hours: Wholesale auctions from 5:30AM, retail from 7AM-4PM daily
voyage.content: The Fish Market is both a trade market for retailers and a place for the general public to get their hands on the day's catch. The fish market has a number of vendors who will cook your fish for you, and a cooking school. Try the local Sydney rock or Pacific oysters. An early lunch at the fish markets is a local institution. Watch out for the swooping seagulls. A shiny new market is under construction right next door

voyage.name: The Little Snail
voyage.hours: Lunch: daily noon–3PM; dinner: Sun-Thu 5:30–9PM, Fri Sat 5:30–10PM
voyage.content: Where else can you have kangaroo marinated and cooked in a French mustard sauce? Try the snails for starter.

voyage.name: Bungalow 8
voyage.content: Tiki bar meets restaurant meets nightclub. Chill out during the day, party by night.

voyage.name: Cargo Bar & Lounge
voyage.content: Perennially packed waterside bar. Caters for a diverse crowd, from younger party-goers to after-work business types, and tourists. Hard to feel out of place there.

voyage.name: Pontoon Bar
voyage.address: Cockle Bay, next to the bridge
voyage.content: Nice views, good on a summer afternoon or warm evening. Busy on Friday and Saturday nights. Basic Australian barbecue food, not too pricey, sausages and salad, etc. Upstairs from Pontoon is the Wallaby Bar, but there is no wildlife, just tributes to the Australian Rugby Union team all around the room. However don't expect a quiet place to watch the rugger, it is a very busy location, with a young crowd, and queues on

voyage.name: Pyrmont Bridge Hotel
voyage.content: Simple, no fuss establishment, popular with the locals and hospitality workers in the area as well. Notable for operating round the clock every day; can get quite rowdy at night after other venues close and hardcore drinkers migrate here.

voyage.name: Slip Inn
voyage.content: Very popular pub. Serves food as well, but worth making a reservation if you intend to eat there.

voyage.name: Pumphouse Bar & Restaurant
voyage.price: Beer from $6 to $30 bottle, pizza around $28, mains in restaurant around $30
voyage.content: Around 10 beers draught on tap, and around 100 available in total. Modern faux-rustic in style, attracts a young after work crowd. Generally busy, but even more after work on a Friday evening. Balcony restaurant upstairs. Pizza served in the bar area. View out onto the courtyard, good for people watching but no water views.

voyage.name: Home
voyage.content: Purpose-built "international super nightclub". Big and international with a cover charge of at least $10 to match.

voyage.name: Base Backpackers Sydney
voyage.price: from $24 for a dorm, $90 for private room
voyage.content: A small Backpackers hostel with dorms & some private rooms. Free Pancake breakfast every morning, and free or low cost activities most days.

voyage.name: Woolbrokers Hotel
voyage.content: A basic, economy hotel on the west side of Pyrmont.

voyage.name: Holiday Inn Darling Harbour Hotel
voyage.content: At the southern end of Sydney's precinct. You can travel around the city area on the local free bus or efficient Light Rail from the nearby stop at Paddy's Markets.

voyage.name: Hotel Ibis Darling Harbour
voyage.content: Economy international hotel, right on the western edge of Darling Harbour, near Harbourside.

voyage.name: Hyatt Regency Sydney
voyage.content: Sydney's largest hotel, with 878 rooms. The interior is nothing to write home about, but the hotel has a great view of the Harbour and a convenient location just off Pyrmont Bridge, with easy access to the CBD as well.

voyage.name: Adina Apartment Hotel Sydney Darling Harbour
voyage.content: Great location, next to King St Wharf on the city side of Darling Harbour.

voyage.name: Novotel Sydney Hotel on Darling Harbour
voyage.content: Great views and the convenience of two modes of public transportation at your doorstep.

voyage.name: The Star Grand Hotel
voyage.content: The obligatory large hotel located in The Star casino complex. Don't expect the kind of accommodation deals you would find in Las Vegas however, unless you quality for admission to the Inner Sanctum.

voyage.name: Central Station
voyage.content: While you can't compare it to New York's Grand Central Station, this Sydney landmark is the busiest and largest station in Australia. The building facade, clock tower and main concourse are the highlights of this station. If you are travelling around on public transport, odds are you may come along the station as it is a major interchange for trains, busses and light rail.

voyage.name: Chinatown
voyage.content: Starts in front of the markets on Hay St and runs just over two blocks to Goulburn St in the north. Dixon St is a malled pedestrian area and closed to traffic. It is decorated in traditional Chinese style and is home to many shops and restaurants. Be sure to explore the surrounding streets for the full experience of Chinatown.

voyage.name: Powerhouse Museum
voyage.content: The Powerhouse Museum is a large museum, essentially of popular culture. It has displays on the history of fashion and transport, decorative arts, music, and space exploration exhibits. It also partly plays on a sci-tech theme, with interactive hands-on and discovery displays of technology, design and industry There is usually a special exhibition on as well. There are in-depth displays for all ages, but also display

voyage.name: White Rabbit Gallery
voyage.content: An Australian gallery dedicated to showing contemporary Chinese art, and claims to have one of the largest collections of it in the world. The teahouse serves an excellent selection of exotic teas along with dumplings and scones. The gallery is often closed in February and August to prepare new installations.

voyage.name: The Goods Line and The Dr Chau Chak Wing Building
voyage.content: The Goods Line is a modern horizontal urban parkland similar to the 'High Line' in New York. The space occupies an unused section of a historic freight line that connected the ports near Darling Harbour to the main railway lines near Central Station. At the park you will find many skaters practicing their tricks and also students from the nearby University of Technology, Sydney. Next to the park is Dr Chau Chak Wing

voyage.name: K-Square Karaoke Lounge
voyage.content: Sing through your favorite K-pop songs, or just your regular top 40 with mates. Drinks and Food also available.

voyage.name: Peter Forsyth Auditorium
voyage.address: Cnr Francis St & Franklyn St, Glebe
voyage.content: Tucked away from Broadway Shopping Centre, this auditorium is used for a wide variety of sports.

voyage.name: Purikura Photoland
voyage.content: One of the largest collections of Japanese claw machines in Sydney. Try your luck in getting a plush.

voyage.name: Capitol Theatre
voyage.content: Housed in a 1920s historical building and host to many theatrical productions, from plays to ballet to musicals like Wicked and Mary Poppins when they come to Sydney.

voyage.name: Chinese New Year Festival
voyage.hours: Held yearly to celebrate the Lunar New Year (varies from Jan to Feb)
voyage.content: The biggest holiday in the East Asian community, it is celebrated with lion dances, fire crackers and dragon boating in the nearby Darling Harbour. The highlight of the festival is the Chinese New Year Twilight Parade, where floats constructed by the local Chinese, Korean and Viet populations travel down George Street. You can also walk a bit further until you hit Circular Quay, where you can see the Opera House go r

voyage.name: Brewery Yard Markets
voyage.content: A small market set on the green adjacent to Central Park shopping centre. This market specialises in street art, crafts, jewelry and clothing with smatterings of food stalls and live music throughout.

voyage.name: Chinatown Night Markets
voyage.content: An open air night market is set up in Dixon Street, selling Asian cuisine, jewellery, clothing, socks, lights, scented candles, sweets and many arts and crafts products. A pale shadow of the markets it is inspired by, but still enjoyable nonetheless.

voyage.name: Paddy's Markets
voyage.content: A famous, large market place in the Haymarket. Lots of clothing, sunglasses, souvenirs, and food. Probably not too many bargains to be had, however. Closest station is Central. Closest bus stop is corner of George and Hay. Light rail stops just outside the door. Parking in Market City.

voyage.name: Capitol Square
voyage.content: A small mall that is best known for Technocity, a maze of over 20 retail stores that focus on electronics; a great option if the Sony store looks a little out of your price range. Many get most of their sales from web front ends or eBay, but it is a very competitive environment to buy computers and electronics. You can also find a few eateries within an arcade filled with games and Purikura photo booths to keep every

voyage.name: Central Park Mall
voyage.content: This shopping centre is part of a larger complex that includes parklands and apartments. There is a wide selection of unique fashion and homeware stores along with general retail and a supermarket. Central Park is also great for its wide range of food and dining options, from cafes to restaurants. If you visit, be sure to check out their website for events that include workshops, art galleries, local markets and the

voyage.name: Market City Shopping Centre
voyage.content: This mammoth place has a fresh produce market on the first level, factory outlets on the second level and more food from more places than you can imagine on the third level. You'll find Paddy's Markets here too.

voyage.name: World Square
voyage.address: Corner of George St and Liverpool St
voyage.content: A large shopping precinct on George St, with many specialty stores, including a Sony Store. Avoid the convenience stores for food and supplies. Coles in World Square is a good place to shop for supplies.

voyage.name: Dixon House Food Court
voyage.address: Corner Little Hay & Dixon Sts, Haymarket
voyage.content: This food court offers a selection of about 20 vendors, with low prices.

voyage.name: Chinese Noodle House
voyage.content: At this intimate, busy eatery decorated with grapes and Persian rugs, the noodles are handmade in traditional northern Chinese style - and the crowds are glad of it.

voyage.name: Hạnh Phúc
voyage.content: Casual Vietnamese vegetarian restaurant with a small menu and "mom and pop shop" vibes.

voyage.name: Menya Noodle Bar
voyage.content: A great restaurant that specialises in ramen. Serves a broth that is not too thin and not too rich; just right. Long queues during weekday lunch hours.

voyage.name: Satang Thai Takeaway
voyage.content: Cheap, tasty and large portions, no need to be picky. There's a reason why a branch with expanded seating has opened right across the street. Particular favourite would be the Pad Thai.

voyage.name: Mamak
voyage.content: Serves Sydney's best roti canai paired with a mouth-warming curry. The teh tarik (pulled tea) and dessert roti are recommended. No reservations are taken, be prepared for queues for up to an hour.

voyage.name: Eating World Food Court
voyage.content: Part of the pagoda-style Harbour Plaza, this food court has a wide range of cheap Asian meals available. Try Gumshara, which sells Japanese tonkatsu ramen, rich with pork collagen.

voyage.name: Sussex Centre Food Court
voyage.content: The food court here has a range of cheap, tasty dishes, making it a sensible choice for those who want to eat and run.

voyage.name: Chat Thai
voyage.content: This restaurant is very busy but offers the very best in Thai cuisine in the city south area. Lines will often stretch out of the restaurant down the street. There is also another branch on the Manly ferry wharf and upstairs in Westfield Pitt Street. Best buys include Pad Thai (sweet, salty & peanuts with lemon juice and rice) and Pork Skewers (ask for pork sticks).

voyage.name: BBQ King
voyage.content: As the name suggests, you come here for barbecue, and a lot of people would agree that this place is king. It's old-school (somewhat dirty), with laminex tables and folding chairs. There may be a queue, but it won't last long, and the great duck is worth the wait. Try the spinach with garlic, too.

voyage.name: Golden Century Seafood Restaurant
voyage.content: With lots of fish tanks displaying your nervous-looking dinner, this place is a favorite late-night eating spot for many of Sydney's chefs and hotel workers. The flavours are exotic and engaging, the service fast and slick.

voyage.name: Marigold
voyage.content: This 800-seat restaurant is a Sydney institution. Serves the hordes yum cha daily for lunch, with service brisk, bordering on rude. Make sure you have a seat close to the centre, or you'll get the leftovers. More laid-back vibe in the evenings. Go for the experience, not the service.

voyage.name: Zilver
voyage.content: Something of a yum cha mothership on weekends, this place offers a mind-boggling array of dishes from the à la carte menu too. Get a group together and have a feast.

voyage.name: Covent Garden Hotel
voyage.content: A local institution. Usually busy, a mix of the after work crowd, tourists, and people in town for a night out. Gets very busy before some shows at the Entertainment centre. It has been renovated in modern style, and struggling a little to recapture the former vibe.

voyage.name: The Bavarian
voyage.content: Reasonable selection of German craft beers though it gets noisy and crowded at peak times.

voyage.name: The Capsule Hotel
voyage.price: $48 for single bed, $86 for double bed
voyage.content: One of a few capsule hotels in Sydney, this one with Sci-fi themed capsules. The reason for the slightly higher cost than most hostels is due to the extra facilities, including TV and safe in your capsule. Day use also available.

voyage.name: The Pod Sydney
voyage.price: From $59 for shared room, $129 for double rooms
voyage.content: While very much a no-frills dormitory, all the beds are king sized. Laundry and kitchen facilities are available.

voyage.name: Sydney Central YHA
voyage.price: From $36 for a shared room, $88 for a private room
voyage.content: Regular events happen throughout the day, and discounted travels to local attractions. Breakfast here only costs $5!

voyage.name: Sydney Railway Square YHA
voyage.price: From $32 for a shared room, $109 for a private room
voyage.content: Also close by to Central station, this YHA offers special $6 dinners every day of the week, and free pancake breakfast on Wednesdays. Wifi and kitchen are available.

voyage.name: Wake Up
voyage.price: Dorms from $32 a night, private rooms from $98
voyage.content: Side Bar is open from 4PM until late every night of the week. The onsite cafe serves budget conscious breakfasts, lunches and dinner. A/C rooms, internet cafe, 24 hr reception, security key card access, storage lockers in dorms, coin operated laundries and a guest kitchen.

voyage.name: Ibis World Square
voyage.content: Located in Chinatown, a 5-minute walk from Central. Very clean rooms and generous breakfast. World Square shopping centre is right across the street.

voyage.name: 28 Hotel
voyage.content: Boutique hotel with minimalist decor evocative of the 1920s. Has an espresso machine in the foyer which any guest can use to make coffee. Minimal frills, good Wi-Fi, and luggage storage are available before check-in.

voyage.name: Mercure Sydney Hotel
voyage.content: 4 star Sydney hotel with 517 rooms, adjacent to Central Station. Easy access to Darling Harbour, Sydney's shopping and retail center and major attractions.

voyage.name: The Capital Hotel
voyage.content: Incorporated within the Capitol Theatre complex. Near Darling Harbour, the Sydney Entertainment Centre, Central Station and Chinatown. Popular with Japanese travellers.

voyage.name: Novotel Sydney Central
voyage.content: Designed for business and holiday travellers. 255 guest rooms and 13 meeting rooms. Guests have access to a bar, outdoor heated pool and a restaurant.

voyage.name: Australian Centre for Photography
voyage.content: ACP established in 1973. The ACP initiated the first major retrospectives of work by photographers such as Max Dupain, Olive Cotton and Merv Bishop, and organised the early public displays of photographs by Bill Henson, Tracey Moffatt, William Yang and Trent Parke and has presented works by international photo-artists such as Bernd & Hilla Becher, Manuel Alvarez Bravo, Larry Clark, Joan Fontcuberta, Nan Goldin, Roni

voyage.name: Australian Museum
voyage.price: free, temporary exhibitions have additional fee
voyage.content: With an international reputation in the fields of natural history and indigenous studies research, community programs and exhibitions, the Australian Museum was established as Australia's first museum in 1827 with unique and extensive collections of natural science and cultural artifacts. The skeleton room, displaying hundreds of animal skeletons, including a blue whale hanging from the roof, is an attraction in itse

voyage.name: National Art School Gallery
voyage.content: The National Art School is housed in a beautiful sandstone prison precinct built in the 1840s.

voyage.name: Sydney Jewish Museum
voyage.price: for adults, for seniors, for students. Children under 10 enter free
voyage.hours: Mon–Thu , Fri , Sun (closed Sat and on certain Jewish holidays)
voyage.content: The museum documents the Holocaust and explores the history of the Jewish people worldwide and also in Australia.

voyage.name: King Street Gallery on William
voyage.content: King Street Gallery on William represents a range of Australian artists, and features changing exhibitions throughout the year.

voyage.name: Roslyn Oxley9 Gallery
voyage.content: The gallery represents over 30 artists, who have had significant shows and whose works are held in major collections nationally and internationally. This gallery has supported work that is challenging and at the forefront of contemporary art practice.

voyage.name: Blender Gallery
voyage.alt: also incorporates The Just Shoot Lomography Shop
voyage.content: Exhibition space over several levels in a typical Paddington terrace. Blender is an outlet for Australian and international photographers, collectors and enthusiasts.

voyage.name: Brett Whiteley Studio
voyage.alt: Look for the big burnt match
voyage.content: Studio of the late Brett Whiteley is now an art museum that is managed by the Art Gallery of New South Wales. The museum is a tribute to the life of Brett Whiteley, considered by many to be one of Australia's most gifted, best known and controversial artists.

voyage.name: El Alamein Fountain
voyage.content: Designed by Robert Woodward and erected in 1961 as a memorial to the Ninth Division during World War II. The fountain has a "dandelion head" sphere of mist at the top of a tall stem and has been imitated globally on many occasions. A favourite meeting place for many travellers and locals.

voyage.name: Paddington Reservoir Gardens
voyage.address: Cnr Oxford St and Oatley Rd, Paddington
voyage.content: Interestingly designed gardens built in the old reservoir.

voyage.name: Elizabeth Bay House
voyage.price: Prices: adult $7, child and concession $3, family $17
voyage.hours: Open Tue-Sun 10AM–4:30PM, closed Mon (except for public holidays), Christmas Day and Good Fri
voyage.content: Built between 1835-1839 and once "the finest house in the colony", this colonial mansion preserves the lifestyle of some of Sydney's wealthiest early settlers, Colonial Secretary Alexander Macleay and his family. Designed by the most fashionable and accomplished architect of the day, John Verge, Elizabeth Bay House is a superb example of colonial architecture and is elegantly and authentically furnished in the style

voyage.name: Moore Park
voyage.price: Open access to all park areas except for groups of 50 or more persons requiring registration and fee payments. Special events may have entry prices fixed by the event managers and special event car parking may attract charges
voyage.hours: The main body of the park is open 24 hrs/7 days per week however some areas may be restricted or annexed as venue sites or parking areas during major events
voyage.content: To the south east corner of this part of Sydney, this 115-hectare open park area has sport fields used by local the local community, bike and walking tracks run through the park area and Kippax Lake, a small lake near the sports stadiums is a pleasant area for picnicking or relaxing on days without major functions in the adjoining facilities. There is one gas-operated barbecue on the western side of Moore Park near S

voyage.name: Rushcutters Bay Park
voyage.address: Adjacent to Royal Cruising Yacht Club and extensive private mooring facilities at Rushcutters bay
voyage.content: Busy on weekends with walkers, people exercising their dogs, picnickers and local people playing informal ball games. The park has a cafe located toward the centre near the water that serves light meals, drinks and other refreshments.

voyage.name: Green Park
voyage.content: A small pleasant area just opposite St Vincents hospital.

voyage.name: Beare Park
voyage.content: A picturesque spot right on the Harbour on Elizabeth Bay, this is a popular place for picnics and a bit of inner-city sunbathing.

voyage.name: Trumper Park Oval
voyage.address: Cnr Glenmore Road and Hampden Street, Paddington
voyage.content: Primarily used for cricket (turf pitch), Trumper Park is also a good quiet spot to relax or get some sun. Between Edgecliff railway station and Trumper Park there is a bushy sloping area where it is possible to camp discreetly away from any public gaze. The toilets in Trumper Park are opened at 5AM. The shops around Edgecliff Railway station have a great range of good value high quality groceries.

voyage.name: Embarkation Park
voyage.content: Great views of the CBD skyline and parts of the harbour. This is one of the most popular places in the Inner East to watch the New Years Eve fireworks shows. The park may be locked at night.

voyage.name: Sydney Gay and Lesbian Mardi Gras
voyage.content: Australia's biggest celebration of gay and lesbian culture, the Sydney Gay and Lesbian Mardi Gras comprises a two-week festival including a fair, exhibitions, fundraising events and parties. The first Mardi Gras was held in 1978, more as a political demonstration. However over the years following it has developed into a large scale cultural festival. The Mardi Gras season culminates in a colourful night-time street p

voyage.name: Oxford St Rock and Roll Walk of Fame
voyage.content: Download the podcast from the City of Sydney website and do a walking tour of past and present landmarks from the Sydney rock'n'roll scene.

voyage.name: Entertainment Quarter
voyage.content: Contains an open air shopping strip, bars and cafes, weekend markets, cinemas, and a number of live television events. It is next to Fox Studios, which is an active film studio and not open to the public. However the nearby entertainment facilities include cinemas, restaurants, bars and promenade areas that are open to the public. There is no entrance charge to access the entertainment quarter. Ample parking in multi

voyage.name: Darlinghurst Gaol
voyage.content: Darlinghurst Gaol was founded in 1822, and is a complex of sandstone penal buildings which now house the National Art School. The complex features several early 19th century sandstone buildings, including a central circular watchtower. There is no signage but the complex is free and open to visitors during business hours. If the large gate on Forbes St is closed, try the gate on Liverpool St. Captain Moonlight, a bus

voyage.name: Hoyts Entertainment Quarter
voyage.address: Building 215, Entertainment quarter, Lang Rd, Moore Park
voyage.content: Cinema experiences and films range from international to local film festivals. Includes IMAX 3D Hollywood blockbusters and documentaries. Facilities for wheelchair-users and hearing-impaired.

voyage.name: Belvoir Street Theatre
voyage.content: Classical and contemporary stageplays.

voyage.name: Griffin Theatre Company
voyage.content: New Australian stageplays.

voyage.name: Hordern Pavilion
voyage.address: The Entertainment Quarter, Lang Rd, Moore Park
voyage.content: With a capacity of up towards 10,000, the Hordern is a common choice for touring bands. It has played host to the likes of Sigur Ros, Interpol and many others. See website for upcoming shows.

voyage.name: Oxford Art Factory
voyage.content: Indie and underground venue, capacity 500-600.

voyage.name: Cook and Phillip Park Aquatic and Fitness Centre
voyage.alt: opposite the north eastern corner of Hyde Park near St Mary’s Cathedral
voyage.price: Adult $6.00, concession $4.50, family $16.00, additional family member $2, spectator $2.70
voyage.hours: Mon-Fri 6AM-10PM, Sat Sun and public holidays 7AM-8PM, closed on Good Fri and Christmas Day
voyage.address: 4 College St, Corner William St, East Sydney
voyage.content: Centre provides world-class swimming, fitness, sporting and recreational facilities including a gym. Sited within a picturesque parkland setting. Swimming facilities include an eight-lane 50-m heated indoor pool and a wave machine.

voyage.name: Andrew (Boy) Charlton Pool
voyage.price: Adult $5.50, concession $4.10, family $15.30, additional family member $2, spectator $2.70
voyage.hours: Sep–Apr, non-daylight saving: daily 6AM-7PM, Daylight Saving: daily 6AM-8PM
voyage.content: A famous yet paradoxically little known location overlooking Wooloomoloo bay and near to the Botanic gardens. It was a popular swimming location with Indigenous Aboriginals before the arrival of Europeans in Australia. The pool was also the venue for the sporting triumphs of Australian swimming legend Andrew Boy Charlton in the 1920s and is believed to be the birthplace of the Australian Crawl or freestyle swimming s

voyage.name: Sydney Roosters
voyage.alt: formerly Eastern Suburbs District Rugby League Football Club
voyage.content: Play in the National Rugby League. Games from March to September, with possible "finals series" (local term for playoff) matches extending as late as October.

voyage.name: New South Wales Waratahs
voyage.content: Play in the Super Rugby competition in rugby union. Games from February to July, with possible finals series matches extending as late as August.

voyage.name: Sydney Swans
voyage.content: Play in the Australian Football League. Games from March to September.

voyage.name: Paddington Markets
voyage.content: Every Saturday 10AM-5PM. Held in the grounds of Paddington Uniting Church, just off Oxford St. Paddington Markets has been in operation since 1973 and is a stylish stall venue for designers, jewellers and craftsmen. Not many true bargains to be had, but perfect for unusual gifts and clothing, as well as some mainstream items. Fantastic for people-watching.

voyage.name: Bar Reggio
voyage.content: Popular East Sydney pizza and pasta restaurant from early evening until late at night. Can be very noisy, but lots of fun for larger groups.

voyage.name: Bill and Toni's
voyage.content: One of the original restaurants of Little Italy on Stanley St. Pastas, but the schnitzel with cheese is a highlight. Have your post-prandial coffee and gelato or cake in the San Siro coffee lounge downstairs.

voyage.name: Tropicana Caffe
voyage.price: Breakfast around $10, focaccias $8-10, salads $10-12 and mains under $20
voyage.content: A Sydney institution, with Ferrari-driving Eastern suburbs socialites rubbing shoulders with taxi drivers. Breakfasts, foccacias, salads, pastas, main dishes, cakes and coffee. The Tropfest short film festival started in this cafe in 1993. Decide what you want from the menu board first, spot a free table and tell the cashier your table number when you order and pay.

voyage.name: China Doll
voyage.content: Asian/Chinese cuisine.

voyage.name: Harry's Cafe de Wheels
voyage.content: A piece of Sydney history, right on the water at Woolloomooloo. Stand up against the van, and grab a pie, peas and mash. There are another couple of franchises open now, in Capitol Square and at the airport. Ignore them, this is the original, and it isn't about the pies. Open early, and late.

voyage.name: Kingsleys
voyage.content: Surf'n'turf. Don't forget your expense card.

voyage.name: Bills
voyage.price: Expect to pay $40-50 for two with coffees and juices
voyage.content: Cafe renowned for its scrambled eggs, sweet corn fritters and ricotta hotcakes. A Sydney favourite when it comes to brunches.

voyage.name: Jazushi
voyage.content: Japanese and European food. There's an open air bar up from the restaurant section with nice seating although a limited selection.

voyage.name: Yulli's
voyage.content: Vegan restaurant.

voyage.name: El Rocco/Bar Me
voyage.content: Sydney's oldest jazz cellar once played host to the likes of Sarah Vaughan and Frank Sinatra. Now it has a small friendly bar upstairs and a downstairs room with regular performances of music, cabaret and comedy. Get some pizza from Bash, the Syrian guy next door.

voyage.name: The East Sydney Hotel
voyage.address: Cnr of Crown & Cathedral Sts, Woolloomooloo
voyage.content: They call themselves the last "Country Pub" in Sydney and are proud to have no poker machines in the building. Nothing fancy here, but the place is relaxed and down-to-earth. Good drinking.

voyage.name: The Tilbury Hotel
voyage.content: A popular spot with the CBD after-work crowd during the week, while on weekends the upstairs balcony is a good place to enjoy some quiet(ish) drinks and music. Food is served in the contemporary style, Italian restaurant downstairs or eat at the bar from the cafe menu.

voyage.name: The Stonewall Hotel
voyage.content: Drag shows, dancing and cocktails. Spread across 3 floors. The bottom floor tends to play the camp 1980s/90s hits and hosts the drag shows, whereas the top two floors play dancier music.

voyage.name: The Colombian Hotel
voyage.content: One of the most popular gay bars in the area, especially with straight people. The beautiful people sit at the open table facing the street to be seen.

voyage.name: Palms
voyage.content: Gay bar/dancing area underground. Music is anywhere between the 1970s and today. Attracts a mixed, generally friendly and unpretentious crowd. Very small, so expect long queues on Saturdays.

voyage.name: Royal Sovereign Hotel
voyage.content: Trendy retro-styled pub with a couple of bars and a bottle shop. A good place for a quiet drink or to get a big night started. There is an outdoor area with a bar on the first floor.

voyage.name: The London Tavern
voyage.content: Cosy local favourite tucked away in amongst the terrace houses of Paddington.

voyage.name: Royal Hotel
voyage.content: Located in a prime position at the Paddo Fiveways, the Royal is a good spot for a drink before having a meal at one of the surrounding restaurants, or at the hotel.

voyage.name: Jolly Swagman Backpackers Sydney Hostel
voyage.content: Safe and clean accommodation with free breakfast, pick up, 24-hr internet access. Friendly staff, but fussy - no refunds or transfers, threaten to throw out your possessions if not left on the bed. Will arrange Sydney day tours and travel including bus passes and east coast packages.

voyage.name: Rushcutters Bay
voyage.alt: Royal Cruising Yacht Club and extensive private mooring facilities are at Rushcutters Bay
voyage.price: Some of the marina and dock areas have restricted access
voyage.address: New South Head Road and New Beach Rd
voyage.content: Rushcutters Bay has many small parks, the largest and most popular being at the southern end of Rushcutters bay. These parks are busy on weekends with walkers, people exercising their dogs, picnicers and locals playing ball games. Rushcutters Park at the southern end has a cafe located toward the centre near the water. To the north west the bay sweeps toward Elizabeth Bay. Further along the bay on the eastern side Ne

voyage.name: Vaucluse Bay Range Front Light
voyage.content: Viewing the lighthouse from the street (80 Wentworth Rd) is very difficult due to the steep terrain so the lighthouse is best viewed from the water.

voyage.name: Vaucluse Bay Range Rear Light
voyage.content: Active lighthouse located on the east side of the entrance to Vaucluse Bay and one of four such lighthouses designed by architect Maurice Festu in a style now sometimes called "Disney Castle".

voyage.name: Harbour Bridge to South Head and Clovelly-walking routes
voyage.price: Brochures are free and all access to the program is free.
voyage.content: A development of the Sharing Sydney Harbour Access Program (SSHAP) including the Sydney Harbour Foreshore Authority and NSW Maritime and Department of Planning. A shared vision to improve public access and enhance the recreational enjoyment of Sydney Harbour and its tributaries for the people of Sydney and visitors to the City. Extensive information and downloadable maps and brochures are available at the website. Th

voyage.name: Kamay-Botany Bay National Park
voyage.content: La Perouse has a museum explaining the interesting history of the area. The Kamay Botany Bay National Park takes its name from the Kamay people (the Spear people) of the nearby Cook's river and Botany Bay. There are walks and great views over the ocean and the bay. The park contains rich marine environments and remnants of the heathland vegetation which Banks and Solander, Cook's botanists, first studied in 1770. You

voyage.name: Bare Island Fort
voyage.content: It sits in the entrance to Botany Bay linked to the mainland by a wooden bridge. Was built to protect the entrance to Botany Bay, and later used as a Veterans Home. Old fortifications and bay views.

voyage.name: Centennial Park
voyage.price: There are no access charges to the park, however some sporting facilities and formal activities may attract fees
voyage.hours: April: 6AM-6PM, May to August: 6:30AM-5:30PM, Sept to Oct: 6AM-6PM, Oct to April: 6AM-8PM. Paddington Gates (exit gate) is the last to close every day
voyage.content: This is a large formal park in Sydney eastern suburbs with its own internal road and walking trail system, grand avenues, historic buildings, lakes and many groves of shady trees dotted with picnic areas. Bike and walking trails, horse trails and equestrian facilities, some restaurant, cafe and kiosk facilities are available. This park is both a playground and a giant green lung for the city. Popular all days but esp

voyage.name: Moonlight Cinema
voyage.alt: is held during the summer months

voyage.name: Cycling
voyage.content: The main circuit is 4 km in length, and there is a separate, much smaller circuit, for children just learning to ride.

voyage.name: Centennial Park Cycles
voyage.content: Cycle hire.

voyage.name: Roller-blading
voyage.alt: Centennial Park is a venue for all levels from children to club competitors

voyage.name: Roller Bladers Total Skate
voyage.content: hire blades

voyage.name: Centennial Park Cycles
voyage.content: Hire blades.

voyage.name: Horse riding track
voyage.alt: Centennial Park is a popular site for horse riding
voyage.content: Centennial Park has a 3.6-km horse-riding track and the Centennial Parklands Equestrian Centre is nearby.

voyage.name: Centennial Homestead
voyage.address: Centennial Homestead, Grand Drive, Centennial Park
voyage.content: Centennial Parklands Dining incorporates a restaurant, café, kiosk and several outdoor areas. Contemporary style menus.
